Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

Felipe, with a photo of the red crit banner reading 'Claude FABLE 7d 100%': 'bottom text is not aligned both vertical and horizontal in relation to banner - slightly upper'. He is right about the vertical, and it is exact arithmetic, not taste.

(a) VERTICAL, the visible defect. screen.cpp:174-179 fills the banner rect at fillRect(5, 116, W-10, 16) — so it spans y=116 to y=131 and its centre line is y=124 — then sets the cursor to y=118. Font0 is 8 px tall, so the glyphs occupy y=118 to y=125 and their centre is y=122. The text sits exactly 2 px high, which is precisely what he is seeing. The correct cursor y is 116 + (16 - fontHeight)/2 = 120. Do NOT hardcode 120: read the font height at runtime (M5.Display.fontHeight()) and compute it from the rect's own y and height, so the two can never drift apart again when someone moves the rect.

(b) HORIZONTAL, a latent bug rather than a visible one — be honest about this in your commit message. The cursor is set to (W - fw)/2, which centres on the SCREEN's midpoint of 120, while the rect spans x=5 to x=235 and happens to share that same midpoint. So today it is centred by coincidence, and the planner measured it off Felipe's photo at roughly 2 px from centre, inside photo error. Centre it on the RECT (rectX + (rectW - fw)/2) rather than the screen, so it stays correct if the rect ever moves or changes width. Same treatment for the 'no hub' branch at screen.cpp:181-187, which is centred on the screen with no rect at all.

While you are in this function, apply the same discipline to the whole footer: every string drawn there should derive its y from one shared baseline constant computed from the footer rect and the font height, not from three separate literals (118, 120, 120 today). One number, one place.

Verify: extract the vertical centring into a pure host-testable helper (given rect y, rect height and font height, return the cursor y) and test it — a 16 px rect with an 8 px font yields 120 for a rect at y=116; an odd leftover rounds consistently; a font taller than the rect clamps to the rect top rather than going negative. Same for horizontal centring within a rect. `make fw-test` Failed 0, `make fw-build` SUCCESS. Then it rides along on the next OTA — do NOT flash, the planner holds that lane and Felipe authorizes each upload. UAT is Felipe confirming the banner text sits centred in the red bar.

description: 12-hour timer backstop with the button as the primary wake (reverses ORDER #29's 60 s): ~9 h of battery becomes weeks, plus the BMI270 suspend ptt proved is mandatory
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

FOUNDER DECISION, and it REVERSES ORDER #29 — Felipe, shown the battery arithmetic, chose '12h backstop - button only'. Record the reversal and its reason in docs/DEVICES.md rather than silently changing the constant, because ORDER #29 argued the opposite and a future reader deserves to know why it flipped.

The measurement that forced it: the planner watched reachability for 12 minutes on battery and got ten clean cycles of ~20 s awake on an 81 s period — the 60 s backstop plus the 20 s grace plus a second of boot. That is a 25 percent duty cycle WITH THE RADIO ON, roughly 27 mA average against a 250 mAh cell: about 9 hours from full. Meanwhile the sibling firmware at ~/dev/felipe/home-automations/devices/m5sticks3/ptt/ptt.ino:49 — the same board, the source this project's teardown was lifted from — uses BACKSTOP_US = 12 hours with the button as the real wake path, and its header records 19 hours of real use costing about 50 percent battery. ORDER #29's 60 s existed so a USB insert would be noticed within a minute; that latency is not worth 720x the wake rate.

(a) CHANGE THE BACKSTOP to 12 hours in armWakeSources (hal/sticks3/power.cpp), keeping ext1 on GPIO11/GPIO12 exactly as it is — the button becomes the primary wake and the timer is a true backstop. Do NOT touch the ext1 pullup_en / pulldown_dis pairing; that is BUG 40's fix and it stays.

(b) ADD THE BMI270 SUSPEND that ptt.ino:205-207 documents as mandatory ('BMI270 suspend — else ~1 mA leak eats the uA win'). Our teardown skips it because internal_imu is false so the sensor is never initialized, and a BMI270 powers on in suspend by default — but that reasoning was written when a missed milliamp cost little. At a 12 hour backstop it is the difference between weeks and days of standby, so write the two registers defensively (0x7D <- 0x00, 0x7C <- 0x03 at address 0x68) rather than trusting the power-on default. Cheap insurance, and it matches the firmware that measured the win.

(c) THE CONSEQUENCE FELIPE MUST KNOW, and it needs to be in the README and docs/DEVICES.md: on battery the device now sleeps until a button is pressed. Plugging in USB while it sleeps will NOT wake it for up to 12 hours — one button press after plugging in restores normal always-on behaviour. This is the same trade ptt makes and it is deliberate, but it will look like a dead device to anyone who does not know, so it must be written down where someone would look.

(d) A TIMER WAKE MUST NOT LIGHT THE SCREEN — verified as a real defect, not a hypothetical. boardInit (board.cpp:22) calls M5.Display.setBrightness(80) unconditionally on EVERY boot, a deep-sleep wake included, and ORDER #31 forces a paint on warm boot. So today a timer wake lights the panel at full brightness for the whole 20 s grace. At a 60 s backstop that was invisible because the device was awake a quarter of the time anyway; at 12 hours it becomes the panel flashing twice a day for an audience of nobody, in a dark room, burning backlight current on top of the wake. FIX: branch on the wake cause, which main.cpp:433 already reads and currently uses only for the dormant ext0 counter. An EXT1 wake (a button — someone is there) or VBUS present lights the screen and paints as it does now. A TIMER wake on battery fetches, refreshes the cached snapshot, and returns to sleep WITHOUT raising the backlight and without painting. Keep emitting [WAKE] either way so the access log from task 61 still sees the request.

Verify: a host test asserting the configured backstop is 12 hours expressed in microseconds (43200000000) and that ext1 still arms both GPIO11 and GPIO12; `make fw-test` Failed 0; `make fw-build` SUCCESS. The real proof is a repeat of the planner's reachability watch on battery: the device must now stay DOWN indefinitely instead of surfacing every 81 seconds, and must come UP on a button press. Do not flash — the planner holds the OTA lane and Felipe authorizes each upload.

PROVEN 2026-09-06 across the day's sessions, all four parts. (a) BACKSTOP: with the 12 h build on battery the device went dark and did NOT return on its own — twice the planner had to ask Felipe to press the blue button to bring it back, which is precisely the UAT ('must stay DOWN indefinitely instead of surfacing every 81 s, and come UP on a button press'). By contrast, on temporary 90 s builds it reappeared every 111 s like clockwork, measured at one-second resolution: 13:49:14 UP -> 13:49:33 DOWN, 13:51:05 UP -> 13:51:24 DOWN. The constant is verified in source as kTimerBackstopUs = 43200000000ULL. (b) BMI270 suspend writes 0x7D<-0x00 and 0x7C<-0x03 at 0x68 in the teardown. (c) SILENT TIMER WAKE: main.cpp computes lightScreen = (wakeCause != Timer) || (vbus >= 4000) and boardInit no longer raises the backlight unconditionally — the device woke, fetched and slept without lighting up, confirmed by the access log recording fetches while Felipe reported the screen dark. (d) The USB-insert consequence is documented. Related and now fixed: the cell would not have survived any of this before task 71, since the board had never charged from USB.

description: Device state reports the requester, not the device: the dashboard shows the browser's own connection, so the StickS3's sleep state is unreachable
steps: Context: usaged (Go, stdlib only) at /Users/fcavalcanti/dev/m5/sticks3-ai-usage. House rules in AGENTS.md. internal/web/ is embedded with go:embed — nothing there is visible until 'make build && launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.fcavalcanti.usaged'.

Task 61 (bbc5d63 + e45f94d) built the access log correctly and then pointed it at the wrong subject. The planner verified the good parts against the running agent: rev and seq hold steady across consecutive requests while count_200 increments, so device_state is genuinely outside the ETag hash; a conditional GET returns 304 with 0 bytes; the token never appears in a log line. All of that stands. The defect is WHOSE state it reports.

THE DEFECT: device_state is keyed by the IP of the client MAKING THE REQUEST (accesslog.go:81 state(clientKey), accesslog.go:146 peerIP, and the usageResponse comment at :137 says so explicitly — 'for the client that made the request'). So when Felipe opens the dashboard on the Mac, the Attention tab shows HIS BROWSER's state, which is permanently 'connected' because the browser is the thing asking. The StickS3's state is not reachable from anywhere. The task existed to answer 'is the device asleep?' and as built it answers 'is the thing currently asking, asking?' — trivially yes, forever. This matters more once ORDER #60's 12-hour backstop ships, because then a sleeping device is the NORMAL state and Felipe has no way to tell it from a dead one.

FIX: track every client as you already do, but expose the DEVICE rather than the requester. Add an endpoint or a field that returns the tracked clients other than the requester — at minimum every non-loopback client, since the browser is loopback and the StickS3 is not. Identify the device positively rather than by elimination where you can: the firmware presents the device token and the loopback browser does not, so a client that has ever presented a valid token is a device. Show each with the fields already built — last seen, seconds since, observed interval, 200/304 split, and the explicit connected/absent/unknown state. The deviceCard in index.html:1211 then renders THE DEVICE, and should say plainly which client it is describing (its address), so there is never ambiguity about whose state is on screen.

KEEP THE INVARIANT THAT ALREADY HOLDS: whatever you add must stay outside the rev hash, and a conditional GET must still return 304 with an empty body. Re-assert it in a test rather than assuming the existing one still covers you.

A NOTE ON PROCESS, because it is the second time: the executor reported 'make verify + make smoke green' but did NOT restart the LaunchAgent — the planner found bin/usaged built at 16:12 while the serving process had been up since 13:44, so none of the work was live and the first verification found no device_state at all. A host task is not done until the running agent serves it. Rebuild AND kickstart, then curl the running agent and paste the actual response in your DONE line.

Verify: `go test ./internal/api ./internal/web -v` grows by at least 4 — a non-loopback client is reported while the requesting loopback client is not mistaken for the device; a client that presented a valid token is identified as a device; the device entry survives the device being absent for hours and reads 'absent' rather than a large number; and a conditional GET still returns 304 with no body. `make verify` and `make smoke` exit 0. THEN REBUILD AND KICKSTART and paste the live curl output. UAT: with the StickS3 on battery and asleep, Felipe opens the dashboard and sees the DEVICE reported as absent with its real last-seen time — not his own browser reported as connected.

CORRECTION after verifying 8693245 against the running agent. What WORKS, confirmed: the agent was rebuilt and restarted properly this time (binary 17:00, process 17:02 — thank you), the access log is live with 85 entries, and it independently reproduces the planner's shell measurement — the device checks in every 80-81 seconds, almost always answered 304. That is the deep-sleep proof Felipe asked for AND independent evidence that the no-redraw contract holds on real hardware. Note for your own debugging: slog writes to usaged.err.log, not usaged.out.log. WHAT IS STILL WRONG: a loopback curl carrying the device token was reported as the device (addr 127.0.0.1), because record() marks isDevice when a client is 'non-loopback OR has ever presented a valid token' (accesslog.go:51-53) and deviceState() then returns the most recent such client. That OR is too loose in BOTH directions and neither case is hypothetical: the ai-usage skill's own refresh command curls LOOPBACK WITH THE TOKEN, and scripts/webui.sh hands Felipe a LAN URL with the token so he can open the dashboard from his phone — which would then be reported as the StickS3. FIX, positively rather than by elimination: the firmware sends NO User-Agent today (fetch.cpp:65 sets only X-Device-Token and If-None-Match), so give it one — 'sticks3-usage/<build id>' — and classify on that. It is a firmware change, but three firmware tasks are already queued for one OTA so it rides along at no extra cost. Until that flash lands, tighten the host rule to non-loopback AND token-bearing AND not announcing itself as a browser (an Accept header asking for text/html, or a Mozilla-style User-Agent). Tests: a loopback client WITH a valid token is NOT the device; a LAN client sending a browser Accept header is NOT the device; a client with the firmware User-Agent IS the device even before it has been seen twice; and with no device seen at all the field is absent rather than falling back to the requester.

SECOND CORRECTION, found by the planner testing 36e9d0a ON THE FLASHED DEVICE rather than in a test. The User-Agent is NEVER SENT. fetch.cpp:64 and :162 use http.addHeader("User-Agent", ua), and the Arduino core REFUSES that header by name: HTTPClient.cpp:1040-1046 skips Connection, User-Agent, Host and Authorization because it manages them itself. The header is silently dropped on the wire — no error, no warning. The correct API is HTTPClient::setUserAgent (HTTPClient.cpp:439). PROOF, not inference: after flashing ddb56c1 and restarting the agent with a clean tracker, the device made check-ins (access-log entries for 192.168.0.136 went 120 -> 121) while device_state stayed ABSENT the whole time. The Go test passed because curl CAN set the header; the device cannot. That is the lesson worth keeping — a test that exercises the server with a hand-made request proves nothing about what the client actually sends.

FIX: replace both http.addHeader("User-Agent", ua) calls with http.setUserAgent(ua) in fetchUsage and refreshUpstream. Then PROVE IT ON THE WIRE, because a second silent drop is exactly the failure mode here: add the User-Agent to the access log line (it is not logged today, which is why this took a source dive to find) and confirm after the next flash that the logged UA for 192.168.0.136 reads sticks3-usage/<build> and that device_state reports 192.168.0.136.

ALSO FIX THE STICKY CLASSIFICATION found alongside it: once an IP has been marked isDevice it stays marked, so a later plain request from that same IP keeps the flag and can win the most-recent-device selection. The planner's own fake-UA curl from 127.0.0.1 poisoned the tracker this way and made a loopback client the reported device until the agent was restarted. Re-evaluate isDevice on EVERY request from the current request's User-Agent rather than latching it, so a client that stops looking like the device stops being treated as one.

description: Freshness lamp: the top-right dot shows data age (green/yellow/red from next_sec) instead of Wi-Fi link, with the server sending the age and the clockless device accumulating its own elapsed time
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

Felipe: 'the top right yellow/green ball should ONLY be controlled like; data fresh? green. data not fresh? yellow. data super stale? red. so, either top refresh button or the wake up blue button or the 12 hourly refresh'. Today that dot is a LINK indicator — screen.cpp:74 paints it green when wifiOk and amber otherwise — which duplicates information the footer already gives as 'no hub'. Repurpose it as the freshness lamp and let the footer keep the link state.

FELIPE'S FOLLOW-UP: 'wifi indicator dif than ball'. The link state does NOT merge into the freshness lamp and does NOT rely on the footer alone — it gets its own distinct indicator in the top bar, visually different from the round ball so the two can never be confused at a glance. Use a SHAPE, not another circle: three ascending vertical bars (1 px wide, heights about 2/4/6 px, 2 px pitch, roughly 7 px total) reads as signal strength at this size and cannot be mistaken for a dot. Solid when the link is up, hollow or dimmed when it is down. Place it immediately LEFT of the freshness ball so the ball keeps the far-right corner Felipe already calls 'top right'. Add it to the existing right-to-left packer in topbar.cpp with its own width and gap, and give it LOWER drop-precedence than the ball: when the bar runs out of room the Wi-Fi bars go first, because a stale-data warning matters more than knowing why. The header has room — centring the page indicator freed the dead space in the middle — but prove it with a layout test at 240 px rather than eyeballing it.

THE HARD PART, and it is why this is not a one-line change: THE DEVICE HAS NO CLOCK. It cannot compute 'how old is this data'. It also does not parse checked_at at all — model.cpp:89 reads only generated_at, which by design moves ONLY WHEN THE DATA CHANGES, so it measures nothing about freshness. A snapshot that is hours stale but unchanged has a generated_at from hours ago and looks identical to one that just changed. Do not try to derive freshness from it.

THE MECHANISM: have the SERVER send the age it alone can compute — seconds since it last polled the providers (now minus checked_at, evaluated at response time) — and have the DEVICE add its own elapsed millis since that fetch. effectiveAge = ageReportedAtLastFetch + millisSinceThatFetch. No clock needed, and it stays correct across a 12-hour sleep because the device knows how long it slept. CRITICAL: that age field must NOT enter the rev hash — it changes every second and would make rev churn constantly, destroying the 304 contract this whole project rests on. Follow exactly the pattern task 61 used for device_state, which the planner verified holds: rev steady across consecutive requests while the unhashed field moves. On a 304 there is no body and no fresh age — that is fine and expected, because the device keeps counting its own millis from the last time it was told.

THE TIERS, derived from next_sec in the snapshot (900 today) rather than hardcoded, so changing the poll interval in the settings page moves them automatically: GREEN while age is at most 2x next_sec; YELLOW up to 4x; RED beyond. A fetch that FAILS does not reset anything, so a device that cannot reach the hub drifts green to yellow to red on its own — which is the correct behaviour and subsumes the old link meaning without a special case. All three of the refresh paths Felipe named reset it naturally: the web refresh button and the device button both POST /v1/refresh so the server re-polls, and a timer wake fetches. Verify that is actually true of the button path rather than assuming it.

Show the same freshness in the WEB dashboard so the two agree — if the device says yellow, the browser must not say everything is fine. Reuse the server-side age directly there, where a real clock exists.

Verify: pure host tests for the tier function (age 0 is green; exactly 2x next_sec is green; one second past is yellow; 4x is yellow; past that is red; tiers move when next_sec changes) and for the age accumulator (a 12-hour sleep followed by a wake yields an age of roughly 12 hours plus whatever the server reported, not zero and not a wrapped value). A test asserting the age field does NOT change rev and a conditional GET still returns 304 with an empty body. `make fw-test` Failed 0, `make fw-build` SUCCESS, `go test ./...` green. Do not flash — batch it with tasks 62 and 63 on the next OTA, which the planner runs and Felipe authorizes.

CORRECTION after reviewing ca9c26c. The design is right and the pieces are right — freshness.h is pure and host-testable, the tiers derive from next_sec, the server sends the age, the topbar gained a separate wifiBars glyph and freshnessDot. One correctness defect, and it fails in the DANGEROUS direction. g_lastFetchMs (main.cpp:124) is a plain static, NOT RTC_DATA_ATTR, and the comment at :122 says the wake path restores model.age and RESETS lastFetchMs to nowMs(). So the sleep duration is discarded by construction: after a 12-hour sleep the device computes restoredAge + ~0 and shows GREEN on twelve-hour-old data. Normally the window is a few seconds because the device fetches on wake — but if that fetch FAILS (no Wi-Fi, hub down, Mac asleep) it sits green on stale data indefinitely, which is exactly the situation the lamp exists to catch. A freshness indicator that is wrong when the data is stale is worse than none, because it converts 'I do not know' into a false reassurance.

FIX, and VERIFY THE HARDWARE FACT RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT: on ESP32 under ESP-IDF, esp_timer_get_time() — what Arduino millis() is built on — is documented to continue across deep sleep, because the RTC timer keeps running and the offset is restored on wake. IF that holds on this board and core (espressif32@6.12.0 / IDF 4.4.7), the fix is simply to move g_lastFetchMs into RTC_DATA_ATTR and STOP resetting it on wake, so nowMs() - g_lastFetchMs naturally spans the sleep. PROVE IT before relying on it: temporarily set the backstop to about 60 s, let the device timer-wake, and log the computed effective age — it must have grown by the sleep duration, not reset to zero. If millis does NOT survive, fall back to storing the effective age in RTC_DATA_ATTR before sleeping and adding the known timer interval on a Timer wake, treating a button wake's unknown duration as at least the elapsed backstop. Say in your DONE line which of the two you found true, with the evidence.

State the honest behaviour in the README: immediately after a wake and BEFORE the first successful fetch, the screen shows the cached snapshot, which genuinely IS old — so the lamp SHOULD read yellow or red at that moment and turn green when the fetch lands. That red-to-green transition is correct and desirable, not a glitch. Do NOT paper over it by forcing green on wake.

Verify: host tests that a 12-hour gap between fetches yields red and NOT green; that a successful fetch immediately after a wake returns the tier to green; that a FAILED fetch after a wake leaves the tier red rather than resetting it; and that accumulateAge neither wraps nor saturates at a 12-hour gap. `make fw-test` Failed 0, `make fw-build` SUCCESS.

THIRD PASS — STILL NOT FIXED, and now the comment asserts otherwise, which is worse than the bug. main.cpp:590 sets g_effectiveAgeAtSleep = accumulateAge(g_dataAgeAtFetch, now - g_lastFetchMs) BEFORE calling powerSleep(). That is the age AT THE MOMENT OF SLEEP. On wake, main.cpp:515-516 restores it and sets g_lastFetchMs = nowMs(). So what survives is the age accumulated BEFORE sleeping — the SLEEP GAP ITSELF IS STILL DISCARDED. After twelve hours asleep the lamp computes roughly the twenty seconds it had accrued before sleeping and shows GREEN on twelve-hour-old data, exactly as before. The comment at :508 claims 'This preserves the sleep duration in the freshness calculation'. It does not. A comment that states the bug is fixed will stop the next reader from checking, so fix the comment as carefully as the code.

THE MISSING QUANTITY IS THE SLEEP DURATION, and the RTC clock is the way to get it — it keeps running through deep sleep, which is the whole reason a timer wake is possible at all. Read the RTC time immediately before powerSleep() and again on wake; the difference IS the sleep duration in real seconds, correct for BOTH wake causes, with no dependence on whether millis() survives. Then effectiveAge on wake = g_effectiveAgeAtSleep + sleepDuration. Store the pre-sleep RTC reading in RTC_DATA_ATTR alongside the age. Do not special-case the timer wake with the 12-hour constant: a button wake has an unknown duration and is the case Felipe will actually hit.

PROVE IT ON HARDWARE, because this has now been reported fixed twice while remaining broken, and host tests have passed every time by exercising accumulateAge directly with a value the wiring never produces. Temporarily set the backstop to about 90 seconds, let the device sleep and timer-wake on battery, and read the effective age the device computes BEFORE its first fetch — it must be roughly 90 seconds larger than it was at sleep, not equal to it. Report the two numbers in your DONE line. Restore the 12-hour backstop before finishing. A host test alone is not acceptable evidence for this one.

HARDWARE PROOF RUN 2026-09-06 — THE RTC APPROACH IS WRONG, and the numbers say why. The planner flashed a temporary uncommitted build with kTimerBackstopUs = 90 s, Felipe unplugged to battery, and the access log captured this:
    13:02:41  200  age_s=4            (on USB, fresh)
    13:06:05  304  age_s=4295195      (after one sleep)
    13:07:55  304  age_s=8590162      (after another)
4295195 seconds is 2^32/1000 — the uint32_t underflow, precisely the signature predicted in ORDER #64: rtcEndMs comes back SMALL against a large g_rtcSleepStartMs. The second value is two wraps accumulated. CONCLUSION: esp_timer_get_time() does NOT survive deep sleep on this board and core (espressif32@6.12.0 / IDF 4.4.7). It was asserted twice — in a code comment and in a DONE line — and the wire disproves it. The lamp would have been stuck red forever, which is the failure direction we were trying to avoid.

THE CORRECT PRIMITIVE IS gettimeofday(). ESP-IDF explicitly maintains system time across deep sleep using the RTC — its own deep_sleep example computes sleep duration by calling gettimeofday() before sleeping and again after wake, which is exactly our need. Replace rtcNowMs(): take a struct timeval before powerSleep(), store it in RTC_DATA_ATTR, take another on wake, and use the difference in seconds as sleepDuration. Keep the g_justSlept guard so a cold boot never uses a stale value, and keep everything else about the design — the effective age still equals g_effectiveAgeAtSleep + sleepDuration.

DEFEND AGAINST THE WRAP REGARDLESS, because a wrong clock must not produce an absurd answer: clamp the computed sleep duration to a sane ceiling (a couple of days is generous against a 12-hour backstop) and treat anything above it as UNKNOWN rather than as a real age. On unknown, show the lamp RED and do not invent a number — red on unknown freshness is honest, 48-days-of-age is not. Add a host test feeding a wrapped delta and asserting it clamps instead of propagating.

Re-prove it on hardware exactly as before — temporary 90 s backstop, unplug, and the access log must show the first age_s after a wake about 90 SECONDS larger than the one before, not 4295195. The planner runs the flash and Felipe the unplug; put the two numbers in your DONE line. Do NOT claim gettimeofday survives deep sleep until that log line exists.

HARDWARE PROOF 2026-09-06 — THE SLEEP DURATION IS NOW COUNTED CORRECTLY. With the 90 s backstop build on battery:
    16:33:11  200  age_s=4      (fresh, immediately after the flash)
    16:35:04  304  age_s=517    wall +113 s
    16:36:55  304  age_s=628    wall +111 s
    16:38:46  304  age_s=738    wall +110 s
Age grows by 111 and 110 against wall gaps of 111 and 111. Had the sleep still been discarded these would have grown by only about 19 s (the awake window); had the clock still wrapped they would read 4295195. gettimeofday DOES survive deep sleep on this board and the accumulation is right. That closes the original defect.
REMAINING DEFECT, visible in the same data: a CONSTANT OFFSET of about 400 seconds. Expected age at 16:35:04 was 4 + 113 = 117; it reported 517, and every later sample is high by the same ~400. The device reported age_s=370 at 16:32:36 immediately BEFORE the OTA flash, and 370 + 35 is about 400 — so the prime suspect is that RTC_DATA_ATTR state survives an OTA REBOOT, not just a deep sleep. If g_justSlept was true when the OTA reboot happened, the wake path adds a sleep duration that never occurred. Deep sleep is not the only thing RTC memory survives. FIX: invalidate the sleep bookkeeping on any boot that is not a deep-sleep wake — readWakeCause() already distinguishes PowerOn from Ext1/Timer, so gate the restore on an actual sleep wake rather than on g_justSlept alone. Add a host test for 'reboot while g_justSlept is set contributes no sleep duration'. Re-prove on hardware the same way: after a flash the first age_s must be close to the server's reported age, not 400 higher.

PROVEN AND CLOSED 2026-09-06. Flashed from a CLEAN worktree at 13c04fc (the executor's in-progress brightness work was deliberately excluded) with a temporary 90 s backstop, device on battery. The server last polled at 17:14:57, so the true data age is measurable independently of the device. Device reports versus truth:
    17:21:23  age_s=387   true 386 s
    17:23:14  age_s=498   true 497 s
    17:25:05  age_s=608   true 608 s
Exact to within a second across three samples, with deltas of +111 and +111 against wall gaps of 111 — so both the ABSOLUTE age and the SLEEP ACCUMULATION are correct. gettimeofday survives deep sleep; the freshness lamp reports the true age of the data.
PLANNER ERROR TO RECORD: the '~400 s offset' filed after the earlier session, and the '~270 s offset' I nearly filed from this one, were BOTH MY MISREADING. I treated the age_s a device sends immediately after a flash reboot as evidence the server had just polled; it is only the device's pre-fetch estimate before the response teaches it the server's real age. The correct baseline is the server's checked_at, not the device's own first report. The executor was sent to fix a defect that probably never existed. Its change — gating the sleep-duration restore on an actual Ext1/Timer wake rather than on g_justSlept alone — is still correct on its own terms and stays, but it was not the reason these numbers are right.

description: Refresh button now 401s on the local dashboard — ORDER #54 over-applied the token requirement to POST /v1/refresh, and the error text blames reading when refreshing failed
steps: Context: usaged (Go, stdlib only) at /Users/fcavalcanti/dev/m5/sticks3-ai-usage. House rules in AGENTS.md. internal/web/ is embedded with go:embed — nothing there is live until 'make build && launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.fcavalcanti.usaged'.

Felipe clicked 'Refresh now' on the local dashboard and got a red banner: '401 Unauthorized — enter your device token to view usage data', with a token entry box. The data itself renders fine because GETs kept the loopback exemption; only the button fails. This is a REGRESSION INTRODUCED BY THE PLANNER'S OWN ORDER #54, which required the device token on every mutating /v1 route even on loopback. That was correct for POST/DELETE /v1/keys and PUT /v1/config — those write his Keychain and rewrite his config, and a cross-site POST to localhost is a real vector. It was WRONG for POST /v1/refresh, which does nothing but ask the agent to poll its providers early. The worst an attacker achieves is a slightly earlier poll. The protection bought nothing and cost the main button on the page.

FIX: exempt POST /v1/refresh from the loopback token requirement, restoring the pre-#54 behaviour for that route ONLY. Keep the token mandatory on POST /v1/keys, DELETE /v1/keys and PUT /v1/config even on loopback — that is the part of #54 that must not be softened, and the live 401 checks the planner ran must still pass for those three. Keep the application/json Content-Type requirement on refresh so a form-encoded cross-site POST still bounces.

ALSO FIX THE ERROR TEXT, which is wrong in a way that would mislead anyone: '401 Unauthorized — enter your device token to VIEW USAGE DATA' appeared while the usage data was already on screen. The failure was a refresh, not a read. Report what actually failed ('could not trigger a refresh') and keep the token prompt for the routes that genuinely need one. A banner that misdescribes the failure sends the reader looking in the wrong place.

Verify: `go test ./internal/api -v` — POST /v1/refresh from loopback with NO token succeeds; POST /v1/keys, DELETE /v1/keys and PUT /v1/config from loopback with no token still return 401; refresh with a non-JSON Content-Type is still rejected. `make verify` and `make smoke` exit 0. THEN REBUILD AND KICKSTART and confirm by clicking the real button in the browser — not by curl alone, since the point is the page.

description: Flash on battery is impossible: upload_ota.sh builds for ~25 s inside the device's 20 s awake window, so espota knocks after it has already slept
steps: Context: usaged (Go, stdlib only) at /Users/fcavalcanti/dev/m5/sticks3-ai-usage; firmware/scripts/upload_ota.sh is the MAC-guarded OTA lane. House rules in AGENTS.md: you never flash — the planner runs this and Felipe authorizes.

Felipe: 'ota only works with device screen on - lmk when you need me to press button'. He is right, and the script makes it worse than it needs to be. On battery the device is awake for the 20 s grace window after a button press, but upload_ota.sh does its MAC check, then rm -f the elf and bin to force a relink, then a full pio run — about 25 s — and only THEN calls espota. The compile consumes the entire awake window, so the invitation arrives at a sleeping device and the flash fails. Today the only workaround is USB, where powerDecide returns StayAwake unconditionally and the device never sleeps.

What is already RIGHT and must not be broken: once a transfer starts it cannot be cut off — main.cpp:554 returns early while otaInProgress(), skipping fetch, render and the sleep decision, so a flash in flight is safe. The problem is purely the window BEFORE espota connects.

FIX: split the script into build and upload phases. Add a flag — --build-only and --upload-only, or a positional phase — so the planner can compile ahead of time (no device needed, no awake window consumed) and then, on Felipe's button press, run only the upload, which starts espota within a second or two. Keep BOTH MAC verifications: one before the build as now, and one immediately before the upload in the upload phase, since that is the guard that stops us flashing someone else's board. The upload phase must refuse to run if no firmware.bin exists or if it is older than the newest source file, so a stale binary can never be flashed silently — that failure would be very hard to diagnose from the device.

Also make the wait explicit rather than a race: in the upload phase, poll the OTA port (3232) for a few seconds and start the moment the device answers, printing something like 'waiting for device — press a button' while it polls. Then Felipe's press and the upload meet reliably instead of depending on human timing.

Verify: `sh firmware/scripts/upload_ota.sh --build-only` produces firmware.bin and touches no network beyond the MAC check; `--upload-only` with a deliberately stale or missing binary refuses with a clear message; the MAC guard still refuses when the host resolves to an unexpected address. Document both phases in firmware/README.md, including WHY it is split — the 20 s battery window — because the reason is the whole point. UAT: the planner flashes the device on battery using the split flow with Felipe pressing a button when prompted.

DEFECT IN THE FIX (b2390a8), found by the planner testing both phases. --build-only works and correctly emits OTA_BUILD_ID and OTA_FIRMWARE. --upload-only IS PERMANENTLY BROKEN BY ITS OWN GUARD: wait_for_ota_port() probes with socket.socket(), which defaults to TCP (SOCK_STREAM), against port 3232 — but ArduinoOTA's invitation listener on 3232 is UDP. The probe can therefore never succeed, and the phase always exits with 'Refusing: device not listening on port 3232 after 10s'. PROOF: with the device awake on USB and the probe refusing, the planner ran espota.py directly against the same IP and port and it uploaded successfully in 31 s. OTA was armed the entire time. A readiness guard that refuses when the device is ready is worse than no guard, and on a battery session it would burn the whole awake window before failing. FIX: do not probe the OTA port over TCP. Either drop the probe and let espota's own invitation retry handle it, or test liveness the way the planner does — an ICMP ping, which is what 'is the device awake' actually means — and then start espota immediately. Keep the MAC guard and the staleness guard, both of which are right. SECOND FINDING for the docs: espota takes about 31 s for this binary, which EXCEEDS the 19 s battery awake window. That is fine and must be explained in firmware/README.md rather than left as a surprise — once a transfer starts, main.cpp:554 returns early while otaInProgress() and the sleep decision is skipped, so only the INVITATION has to land inside the awake window. Re-verify by flashing the device on battery with the split flow end to end.

PROVEN ON HARDWARE 2026-09-06 (7e0f993). The ICMP fix works and the split flow did exactly what the task was created for: the planner pre-built the binary with no device involved (28 s), Felipe unplugged to battery and pressed the blue button, and the upload phase — polling at 2-second resolution — caught the wake and completed 'OTA upload complete'. Also verified: --build-only emits OTA_BUILD_ID and OTA_FIRMWARE for the caller; the staleness guard correctly REFUSED a stale binary when screen.cpp was newer, naming the offending file; the MAC guard runs in both phases. A battery flash is now routine instead of impossible.

description: RETRACTED (false premise): 'device never fetches on battery' was a logging failure, not a device fault — kept only as the record of how a hand-started server produced a wrong conclusion twice
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

Measured by the planner on 2026-09-06 with a temporary 90 s backstop build (7ffc461 + uncommitted 90 s constant), Felipe on battery. Reachability sampled once per second:
    13:49:14 UP -> 13:49:33 DOWN   (19 s awake)
    13:51:05 UP -> 13:51:24 DOWN   (19 s awake, 111 s period)
So deep sleep, the timer backstop and the wake all work. But across TWELVE MINUTES of this cycling the access log recorded ZERO requests from 192.168.0.136. The device is awake for 19 seconds with Wi-Fi joined — ping answers, so it has an IP — and it never asks the server for anything.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE TEST IT BLOCKED: on battery the device never refreshes its data at all. It shows whatever it last fetched on USB, for as long as it stays on battery. Every wake is spent joining Wi-Fi and going back to sleep having learned nothing. That defeats the point of waking, and with the 12 h backstop from ORDER #60 it means a battery device is permanently stale rather than merely infrequently updated.

Where to look, from a black-box reading of the code — do not assume, instrument it. pollUpdate (main.cpp:324) fetches on one of two paths: a first fetch when g_nextPoll == 0 and now - g_netUpAt >= kFirstFetchDelayMs (3 s), or a periodic poll when now >= g_nextPoll. g_nextPoll is a plain static so it IS zero on wake, and 19 s of awake time is ample for a 3 s delay — so on paper the first-fetch branch should fire every cycle. It does not. Candidates: netUp() never becomes true within the window even though ping works; g_netUpAt keeps resetting because netUp() flickers during association; the fetch fires but fails before reaching the server (DNS, ARP, or a TCP connect that outlives the grace window); or the grace anchor expires from a different origin than you expect on a silent wake.

FIX THE BEHAVIOUR, not just the symptom: on a wake, fetch AS SOON AS the network is usable rather than after a fixed 3 s delay, and RETRY within the awake window instead of giving up after one attempt — a single failed attempt currently costs the entire cycle. If the grace window can expire mid-fetch, hold sleep off while a fetch is genuinely in flight, the way the OTA guard already holds it off (main.cpp:554). A wake that does not result in a fetch is a wasted wake and should be treated as a failure worth reporting, not silence.

MAKE THE WAKE OBSERVABLE WITHOUT SERIAL, because there is no cable and black-box diagnosis has now hit its limit twice. The device should tell the server it woke even when the snapshot fetch fails — for example include the wake cause and a wake counter as query parameters alongside the age_s you already send, and log them. Then a wake that produced no data still leaves a trace, and the difference between 'never woke', 'woke but never asked' and 'asked and failed' becomes a log grep instead of a guess.

Verify on hardware, since that is the only thing that counts here: with a temporary 90 s backstop and the device on battery, the access log must show a request from 192.168.0.136 on EVERY wake — roughly one every 110 seconds — each carrying age_s. Host tests for the retry logic and for 'fetch in flight blocks sleep'. Then task 65's proof can finally run: the first age_s after a wake about 90 seconds larger than the one before.

RETRACTION 2026-09-06, and the error was the planner's. The 'zero requests' finding was measured against an access log that NOTHING WAS WRITING TO. A hand-started ./bin/usaged serve (pid 60384) held port 8765 outside launchd — the SECOND occurrence of the same problem in ninety minutes, after the first was flagged at room seq 337 — so its stderr went to whatever terminal launched it while launchd sat in 'spawn scheduled' unable to bind. Serial told the truth in one capture: [FETCH] code=304 rev=9d41d07e ms=202 at the 300 s boundary, and a cold-boot [FETCH] code=200 ms=74. After killing the stray and restoring the LaunchAgent, the very next poll logged normally: 14:22:07 200 age_s=778 sticks3-usage/39f8279. THE DEVICE WAS FETCHING THE WHOLE TIME. No firmware change is required and none should be made from this task. Two lessons worth keeping: an absence of evidence in a log is not evidence of absence until you have confirmed WHO IS WRITING THAT LOG; and the serial cable, which we had treated as retired, answered in one capture a question that black-box observation had failed twice.

description: Battery discharges while plugged into USB: charging is never enabled or configured, and the [BATT] line cannot tell charging from draining
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

Measured by the planner over serial on 2026-09-06 while the device sat on USB with VBUS at 5280 mV and usb=1 reported on every line:
    14:13  [BATT] pct=97 v=4094 usb=1
    14:15  [BATT] pct=93 v=4050 usb=1
    14:30  [BATT] pct=88 v=4008 usb=1
    14:31  [BATT] pct=86 v=3992 usb=1
Roughly one percent per minute of DISCHARGE while plugged in. Power is unquestionably present — VBUS reads 5280 mV and the USB branch of powerDecide keeps the device awake — so the cell is simply not being charged faster than the device draws. This is why the battery keeps arriving flat for hardware sessions: 'plugged in' has not meant 'charging'.

THE FIRMWARE NEVER CONFIGURES CHARGING. M5Unified exposes setBatteryCharge(bool), setChargeCurrent(uint16_t) and isCharging() (Power_Class.hpp:153, :158, :167) and our code calls NONE of them — charging is left to whatever the M5PM1 does by default. Enable it explicitly at boot and set a charge current appropriate for the 250 mAh cell (a conventional 0.5C to 1C gives roughly 125-250 mA; choose deliberately and write down why). Verify the API is actually implemented for the M5PM1 in this M5Unified version rather than assuming — a grep of Power_Class.cpp for m5pm1 alongside charge found nothing, so it is possible these calls are no-ops on this PMIC. IF THEY ARE NO-OPS, say so plainly and write the PMIC registers directly, the way the teardown already writes ES8311 and BMI270 registers. Do not report success on an API that silently does nothing — that is the same shape as the addHeader(User-Agent) bug.

MAKE IT OBSERVABLE, since 'usb=1' currently tells us power is present and nothing about whether it is helping: add the charge state to the [BATT] serial line and to the battery telemetry — isCharging() where available, otherwise the sign of the voltage trend over a few samples. A line that says usb=1 while the cell drains is actively misleading, and it is what let this go unnoticed through several sessions.

Verify on hardware, which is the only thing that counts: with the device plugged in and awake, the serial [BATT] line must show pct and voltage RISING over ten minutes, not falling, and must report a charging state. Then confirm the device still sleeps correctly on battery afterwards — charge configuration must not interfere with the teardown or the wake sources. Report the before and after voltages in your DONE line.

HARDWARE PROOF 2026-09-06, run by the planner over serial after flashing eb533df. Before the fix the cell drained on USB at about one percent per minute. After: [BATT] pct=86 v=3994 usb=1 chg=0 at 39 s, still chg=0 and falling at 129 s (pct=85 v=3986), then chg=1 from 189 s onward with pct climbing 92, 94, 97, 99 and voltage 4042 -> 4096 mV across ten minutes. Root cause confirmed as reported: M5Unified's board init for the M5StickS3 configures GPIO0 as the CHG_STAT input but never calls setBatteryCharge(true), so the PM1 CHG_EN bit stayed clear and the board had NEVER charged from USB. The commit is also honest about its limits, which is why it is trusted: it documents that setChargeCurrent and setChargeVoltage are stubs on the M5PM1 and that the real current comes from the hardware CHG_PROG resistor.

description: Brightness control from the device: double-click the blue button for a gauge, blue brightens, side dims, 25 percent default, persisted — and reserve the blue hold for a future AI-agent action
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

Felipe, verbatim: 'theres NO way of controling the brightness. We could do by double click front blue button, gauge appears.... if press blue (same) brightness increases... if press big side button (not the reset) brightness decreases. probably a good default to start is 25%. leave this for the end, but anotate.' DEFERRED BY HIS INSTRUCTION — this is queued behind the open hardware work (task 65's freshness proof, task 69's OTA split). Do not start it before those.

Today brightness is two compile-time constants: kBrightnessActive = 80 of 255 (about 31 percent) and kBrightnessIdle = 20, with a 30-minute idle dim (main.cpp:62-64, updateBrightness at :387). Changing it needs a reflash. It is also the largest backlight draw on a 250 mAh cell, so this is a battery feature as much as a comfort one — quantify that when you are done.

BRIGHTNESS MODE, entered by double-clicking BtnA: a gauge overlay shows the current level; BtnA click steps brighter and BtnB click steps dimmer through discrete levels (5/10/25/50/75/100 percent mapped onto the 0-255 range M5GFX takes); while in the mode BtnA must NOT cycle pages and BtnB must NOT refresh; it exits after a few seconds of inactivity and saves on exit rather than on every press. BtnB HOLD must still flip the screen even inside brightness mode, or the way out is confusing.

PERSISTENCE: reuse the existing NVS pattern rather than inventing one — Preferences with the namespace 'usaged', exactly as loadRotation/saveRotation do at board.cpp:96. Add a 'bright' key, validate it on load and fall back to the 25 percent default, the same way rotation validates to 1 or 3. It must survive a reboot AND a deep-sleep wake.

IDLE DIM INTERACTION, easy to get wrong: updateBrightness currently snaps between two constants. The user's chosen level becomes the ACTIVE level and the idle state must dim RELATIVE to it — otherwise choosing 5 percent would make the idle state brighter than the active one, which is absurd on its face and would not show up in a test that only checks two fixed numbers.

THE ONE REAL TRADEOFF, and Felipe should feel it before we decide: telling a single click from a double click needs wasSingleClicked() instead of wasClicked() (both exist, Button_Class.hpp:28 and :31), which adds roughly a quarter second of latency to PAGE CYCLING — the most-used gesture on the device. Implement it as specified, then judge it in the hand. If it feels sluggish, the fallback is to move brightness onto a BtnA hold instead, which frees the double-click but collides with the refresh currently bound there.

ANNOTATE ONLY, DO NOT BUILD: Felipe wants BtnA HOLD reserved for a future action that reaches an AI agent / Claude Code. Record that in docs/DEVICES.md beside the button map so the gesture is not spent on something else. Note the consequence there too — the refresh currently on BtnA hold needs a new home, and since BtnB click already refreshes it can probably just be dropped.

ALSO RESOLVE, since it is adjacent and cheap: Felipe reports the blue button hold 'does nothing', but main.cpp:310 binds BtnA hold to doDeviceRefresh gated on netUp(). Diagnose it over SERIAL using the [BTN] lines rather than guessing — the likely candidates are the netUp() gate, the 10-second refreshThrottleOk window silently swallowing the press, or drawRefreshStatus() being too brief to notice. If it turns out to be only a feedback problem, say so; that is a much smaller fix than it looks.

Verify: host tests for the level stepper (clamps at both ends, steps in order) and the mode state machine (entry, exit on timeout, BtnB hold still flips, BtnA does not cycle pages while in the mode) — same shape as test_hold_flip.cpp. `make fw-test` Failed 0, `make fw-build` SUCCESS. Then hardware UAT with Felipe: double-click blue brings the gauge, blue brightens, side dims, it exits on its own, the level survives a reboot and a deep-sleep wake, and page cycling still feels responsive. Finally confirm on serial that a lower level measurably slows the discharge, using the same [BATT] voltage-trend method that proved the charging fix.

FLIP REVERTED by the planner. The executor flipped this on the strength of Felipe's 'works perfect', but that same UAT message raised two defects which became task 74: the gauge tick labels piling up at the left end, and — verbatim about the instructions screen — 'maybe letters are almost too big. The first two phrases are trampled on each other... They are not that good on the instructions screen.' A task whose own UAT produced complaints is not passing until the fix for those complaints is confirmed on hardware. Task 74 (cd50477) is flashed and awaiting Felipe's eyes; these two flip only after he confirms.

UAT PASSED 2026-09-06 on cd50477 (built while the device slept, uploaded on Felipe's button press via the split OTA flow). Felipe's verdict on the gauge and the instructions page after the task-74 fixes: 'perfect.' All three flip together because they are one feature and its fix: brightness stepping with the evenly-spaced index ticks, the instructions page derived from kBindings with shortened words, and the measure-and-fit guard that keeps a future binding edit from reintroducing the overlap. The geometry is now locked by host tests rather than by eye — every kBindings entry must fit 240 px with a gap, and the six gauge positions must be evenly spaced and non-overlapping.

description: Instructions page: a final page in the cycle showing what the buttons do, in large type, generated from the real bindings so it cannot drift
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

Felipe: 'last screen - instructions, big letters'. Add one more page at the END of the page cycle whose whole job is telling you what the buttons do. The footer hint is 29 glyphs of 6-pixel font squeezed beside the version — it can never carry this, which is why the hold-to-flip gesture was undiscoverable until he was told about it. Queue this with task 72 (brightness); they change the same button map and should ship on one flash.

BIG LETTERS IS THE REQUIREMENT, not a suggestion. The screen is 240x135 and the rest of the UI uses Font0 at 6 px because it packs data; this page carries about five short lines, so use a substantially larger font and let it fill the space. If a line does not fit, shorten the WORDS rather than the font — 'FLIP' beats a smaller 'ROTATE SCREEN'. Reuse the existing measure-then-fit helpers (textfit, and centerTextX/centerTextY from align.h) rather than hand-placing pixels.

CONTENT is the current binding set, in plain language: blue click cycles pages, side click refreshes, side hold flips the screen 180 degrees. Once task 72 lands, blue double-click enters brightness. Do NOT hand-write this list as a string literal — DERIVE IT FROM THE SAME TABLE the button handler uses, or add such a table if none exists, so a future binding change cannot leave the help page lying. A help screen that disagrees with the hardware is worse than none, and this project has already shipped one stale hint ('side: refresh' after the side button also gained flip).

PAGING BEHAVIOUR: it is the LAST page, reached by cycling past the data pages, and the page indicator must count it (so 1/4 becomes 1/5). It must not become the boot page, must not be the page a wake lands on, and must not be what Felipe stares at when he glances over — the device exists to show quota. description: PROVISIONING 0/4: SPIKE — answer the five unknowns on real hardware before any of 76-79 is written
steps: Firmware context: M5StickS3 unit #2, hostname sticks3-usage. PlatformIO espressif32@6.12.0 / Arduino core 2.0.17 / ESP-IDF 4.4.7, M5Unified 0.2.19 + M5GFX 0.2.28. Purity rule: gesture LOGIC goes in the pure core (firmware/src/usage/, no M5 or Arduino headers, host-tested by 'make fw-test'); only firmware/src/hal/sticks3/* and main.cpp may touch M5. Flash this over OTA ('make fw-ota'), no cable. Any upload needs Felipe's explicit authorization in the Solvr room.

WHY THIS EXISTS (read once, applies to all four provisioning tasks): secrets.h is a COMPILE-TIME header, so WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS, USAGED_HOST, USAGED_DEVICE_TOKEN and OTA_PASS become plaintext strings inside firmware.bin — verified with `strings` against a real build. Publishing that binary to M5Burner would hand out the builder's Wi-Fi password, and a stranger's flash could not work anyway because it would try to join OUR SSID and reach OUR Mac. The goal of this group is a binary that carries NO credentials and a device a stranger can set up without a cable, a build step, or a file. THE DECISIVE CONSTRAINT: every off-the-shelf provisioning framework (Espressif WiFiProv, Improv, WiFiManager) conveys Wi-Fi CREDENTIALS ONLY. This device additionally needs to learn WHICH AGENT to talk to and to obtain a DEVICE TOKEN, so a custom portal that collects all four in one screen beats a generic app that solves half and leaves a second setup step. Build order matters and is not negotiable: credentials store first, then the portal that fills it, then pairing, then the everyday editing path. A pairing code cannot help a device that is not yet on the network.

WHY A SPIKE FIRST. Tasks 76-79 are specced but rest on five assumptions that are documented rather than measured. Every single defect that cost real time on 2026-09-06 had that exact shape: addHeader('User-Agent') is documented to set a header and the Arduino core silently drops it; esp_timer_get_time is documented as monotonic and does not survive deep sleep; a readiness probe against port 3232 looked obvious and was TCP against a UDP listener; M5Unified is documented to manage the PMIC and never enables charging. Four for four. THROWAWAY CODE ONLY — this spike answers questions and is then DELETED; do not let it become the implementation, and do not commit it to src/.

Q1 — DOES THE PORTAL STACK EVEN FIT AND RUN? Bring up WiFi.softAP with WebServer and DNSServer together and report the flash and RAM delta against today's baseline (about 31 percent of the app partition, RAM 16.6 percent). If it does not fit comfortably alongside the existing firmware, every later task changes shape, so this is the first question.

Q2 — CAN IT SCAN WHILE THE AP IS UP? WiFi.scanNetworks() while running as an access point requires WIFI_AP_STA and is widely reported as unreliable — scans returning empty, or the AP dropping its client mid-scan. The portal is USELESS without a network list, so measure it: scan repeatedly with a phone attached to the AP and report how often the list is empty and whether the client survives. If it is flaky, the fallback design is scan-before-AP with a cached list plus a manual-entry field, and that changes task 77's page.

Q3 — DOES THE CAPTIVE SHEET ACTUALLY POP? Wildcard DNS plus the platform probe endpoints (Apple hotspot-detect, Android generate_204) are supposed to trigger the automatic sign-in sheet. In practice this is notoriously version-dependent. Test on Felipe's ACTUAL iPhone and on an Android device if one is available. Report per platform: does it pop by itself, or does he have to open a browser and type the IP? A portal most people never find is not a portal, and the answer decides whether task 77 needs on-screen 'open your browser and go to …' instructions as the primary path rather than a fallback.

Q4 — CAN WE SKIP ALL OF IT? M5Burner has its own Wi-Fi configuration step that injects credentials at flash time rather than into the binary. Find out WHERE it writes them — which NVS namespace and keys — and whether an ordinary Arduino sketch can read them. IF IT CAN, a published build could arrive pre-configured and tasks 77 and 79 shrink dramatically. It may well be UIFlow-specific and turn out to be nothing, but it is the cheapest question here and the only one that could delete work rather than add it. Answer it early.

Q5 — REBOOT OR RUNTIME SWITCH? Determine whether going from AP to station mode needs a reboot or can be done live, and whether NVS writes survive it cleanly. A reboot is perfectly acceptable during setup and much simpler; confirm it rather than assume it, and confirm the credentials written just before the reboot are actually there after it.

Verify: this task produces a WRITTEN ANSWER to each of Q1-Q5 posted in the room and appended to docs/DEVICES.md, with measured numbers rather than expectations — flash and RAM delta, scan success rate, per-platform captive behaviour, the M5Burner finding, and the transition result. Then AMEND tasks 76-79 to match what was learned, and say explicitly which assumptions survived and which did not. The spike branch or scratch sketch is then deleted. Nothing in 76-79 starts until these answers exist — that is the entire point.

Define the on-device credential record and its NVS storage, reusing the Preferences pattern already proven by loadRotation/saveRotation in board.cpp (namespace 'usaged'): wifi_ssid, wifi_pass, agent_host, agent_port, device_token, and ota_pass. Every field validated on load with a safe fallback, exactly as rotation validates to 1 or 3. A record is COMPLETE only when ssid, agent_host and device_token are all present; anything less means the device is unprovisioned and must enter the portal rather than silently retrying a half-configuration.

The state machine is a PURE C++17 module in src/usage/ with no M5, WiFi or Arduino headers — same discipline as hold_flip.{h,cpp} and freshness.{h,cpp}, so it is host-testable. States: Unprovisioned (no complete record) -> Portal; Provisioned -> Joining; Joining -> Online on success; Joining -> Retry with backoff on failure; and after N consecutive failed joins -> Portal, so a moved house or a changed password does not require a USB reflash. That fallback is the whole reason the machine exists — WITHOUT IT the only recovery is a cable, which is precisely what this work removes.

SECRETS MUST LEAVE THE BUILD. secrets.h becomes optional and, when present, is treated as a DEVELOPER CONVENIENCE ONLY: a seed used to pre-populate NVS on first boot, never a runtime source. The production build must compile with NO secrets.h at all and produce a binary that contains none of the five values. Add a build-time or CI check that greps the resulting firmware.bin for each configured value and FAILS if any is found — this is the check that makes a published build safe, and it is the one thing in this group that must never regress.

Verify: host tests for the record's completeness rule, for each field's validation and fallback, for the state transitions including the N-failures-to-Portal path, and for the rule that a partial record never counts as provisioned. `make fw-test` Failed 0 and `make fw-build` SUCCESS. Then the security assertion, which is the real deliverable of this task: build with no secrets.h and confirm with `strings firmware.bin` that no SSID, password, host or token appears. No device needed for any of this.

AMENDED BY SPIKE (2026-09-06) — task 75 measured these; they change this task. (1) THE LEAK IS FIVE VALUES, NOT FOUR: WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS, USAGED_HOST, USAGED_DEVICE_TOKEN and **OTA_PASS** all appear verbatim in firmware.bin (re-verified with strings against a real build). The CI/build check must cover all FIVE. (2) CONCRETE EDIT THE ORIGINAL TEXT NEVER NAMED: firmware/src/hal/sticks3/net.cpp:9-15 carries TWO #error guards that hard-require secrets.h. Making secrets.h optional means removing them, not just changing how the values are read. (3) THE NVS NAMESPACE IS "usaged", NOT "usated" — docs/DEVICES.md:133 had a typo (now fixed) while board.cpp:98,111,123,136 and board.h:45,53 all use "usaged". Reusing the wrong namespace would silently lose every stored value. (4) NVS DURABILITY IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: a Preferences write issued immediately before ESP.restart(), with no clean shutdown, read back identical after the reboot (reset_reason=3). Writing credentials and rebooting straight away is safe. (5) The strings check path from the repo root is firmware/.pio/build/m5stack-sticks3/firmware.bin — '.pio/' does not exist at the root, and an empty result from the wrong path reads exactly like 'no leak'.

WHY THIS EXISTS (read once, applies to all four provisioning tasks): secrets.h is a COMPILE-TIME header, so WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS, USAGED_HOST, USAGED_DEVICE_TOKEN and OTA_PASS become plaintext strings inside firmware.bin — verified with `strings` against a real build. Build order matters and is not negotiable: credentials store first, then the portal that fills it, then pairing, then the everyday editing path. A pairing code cannot help a device that is not yet on the network.

When the state machine says Unprovisioned, the device brings up its own access point and serves a one-page portal. The AP SSID must be unique per device — derive it from the MAC, e.g. 'usaged-A4F2' — and the AP must be WPA2-protected rather than open, with the SSID AND the AP password shown ON THE DEVICE SCREEN. The screen is the reason we can do this properly: an open AP lets a neighbour reach the setup page, and a printed password would need a label. Show a short instruction line too, in the large type task 73 established.

The portal page collects everything in one screen: a LIVE SCAN of nearby networks as a pick-list, a password field, and the agent's address and port. Offer mDNS discovery of the agent if it is cheap, but always allow a manual address — discovery that silently fails is worse than a field. Include a 'join manually' path for HIDDEN SSIDs, which never appear in a scan. CRITICAL AND OFTEN MISSED: the ESP32-S3 radio is 2.4 GHz ONLY, so a 5 GHz-only network or a band-steering SSID simply will not appear. When the scan finds nothing, the page must SAY THAT — an empty list with no explanation is the single most confusing possible outcome for a new user.

MECHANICS, so this is not rediscovered: the Arduino core already ships everything needed — WiFi.softAP for the access point, WiFi.scanNetworks for the list, WebServer for the page, and DNSServer for the wildcard hijack; WiFiProv and BLE are also present but are NOT used here, for the reason in WHY above. Decide and state whether the AP-to-station transition is a reboot or a runtime mode switch — a reboot is far simpler and entirely acceptable during setup, and the state machine from task 75 already handles a cold boot into Joining. Watch the flash budget: the build sits near 31 percent of the app partition today, so there is ample room, but report the delta in your DONE line. And keep the portal OFF the normal path — it must not run, listen, or cost memory once the device is provisioned.

Make it a real captive portal, not just a web server: run a DNS server that resolves every name to the device, so a phone's connectivity check redirects into the page automatically. Handle the platform probe URLs (Apple's captive.apple.com hotspot-detect, Android's generate_204) so both iOS and Android pop the sheet by themselves. A portal the user has to find by typing an IP is a portal most people never reach.

On submit: validate, write the record via task 1's store, show the outcome ON THE SCREEN, then drop the AP and join. If the join FAILS, return to the portal with the reason visible rather than rebooting into a loop — the failure case is the one the user will actually hit, with a mistyped password. Never render a submitted password back to the page, and never log it.

Verify: pure host tests for the page-building and form-validation logic (the parts with no radio in them), including the empty-scan message and rejection of an incomplete submission. `make fw-test` Failed 0, `make fw-build` SUCCESS. Then the hardware UAT, which only Felipe can run and which is the point of the whole task: starting from a device with NO stored credentials, he joins the AP from a phone, sees the portal appear BY ITSELF, picks his network, enters the password and the agent address, and the device joins and starts fetching — with no cable, no build, and no file edited. Report the flash and the join in the room; do not flip passes until he confirms.

AMENDED BY SPIKE (2026-09-06) — measured on unit #2; several assumptions in this task were wrong or under-specified. (1) IT FITS, MEASURED: the portal stack costs +28,736 bytes of flash (31.4% -> 32.2% of the app partition) and about 53 KB of heap (315,452 B free at boot -> ~262,700 B with SoftAP+DNSServer+WebServer serving). Minimum heap with a client mid-request was 249,028 B. Flash and RAM are NOT constraints here. (2) KEEP THE LIVE SCAN — the scan-before-AP fallback this task hedges about is NOT needed. Across every client-attached window on both an Android and an iPhone: 0 empty scans, 0 failures, 0 disassociations, still finding 27-33 networks with the phone associated. Across ~90 scans: 1 empty (1.1%) and 5 WIFI_SCAN_FAILED (5.6%), every failure OUTSIDE a client window and clustered at boot/AP reconfiguration. (3) BUT USE THE ASYNC SCAN: the synchronous WiFi.scanNetworks() waits on a HARDCODED 10 s (WiFiScan.cpp:95), not on max_ms_per_chan. Use scanNetworks(async=true) plus scanComplete() polling. (4) DISTINGUISH WIFI_SCAN_FAILED (-2) FROM AN EMPTY SCAN (0). Both occur. -2 means 'the radio refused, retry'; 0 means 'genuinely nothing here, explain 2.4 GHz'. Rendering -2 as 'no networks found' would be actively misleading. (5) THE CAPTIVE SHEET AUTO-POPS ON BOTH PLATFORMS — confirmed on the wire, not just by eye: [PROBE] apple host=captive.apple.com hitting /hotspot-detect.html, and [PROBE] android host=connectivitycheck.gstatic.com, each arriving 3-6 s after association with no browser opened. The wildcard DNS hijack works on both. The sheet can be the PRIMARY path; keep on-screen instructions as a real fallback (one handset each is not a survey and this is famously version-dependent). (6) DECISIVE, AND IT CHANGES THE UX: AP_STA IS SINGLE-CHANNEL (esp_wifi.h:812-813 — the soft-AP adopts the station's channel). The moment the device joins the target network the portal AP hops channels and the phone is DROPPED. Any design that shows a 'connected!' page in the browser after the join is impossible. Show the outcome ON THE DEVICE SCREEN. (7) NO REBOOT IS NEEDED to leave AP mode: WiFi.mode(WIFI_STA) from AP_STA returned true with the station connection untouched (staStatus=3, same IP). A reboot is also fine — cold boot to fully operational (STA joined, OTA armed, AP up, DNS+web serving) took 3 s. (8) MECHANICS THAT WILL OTHERWISE BE REDISCOVERED THE HARD WAY: register the OS probe paths BEFORE any catch-all (first match in registration order wins, chosen from the request line before a single header is read, so you cannot route on Host); do NOT send(204) for Android (the header builder still emits Content-Type and Content-Length, i.e. the 'no portal' answer) — send a 302 to the AP IP; NEVER call onFileUpload() on the portal server (it makes the handler claim every non-GET body via the raw path and arg() comes back empty); ADD A /favicon.ico HANDLER (unhandled it logs a core error and costs an extra TCP round through a server that takes ONE client at a time); keep the page to ONE self-contained document (every response carries Connection: close); read the AP IP back with WiFi.softAPIP() rather than hardcoding 192.168.4.1 (that default lives in precompiled esp_netif code); the softAP password minimum is 8 chars or softAP() returns false; use WiFi.macAddress() NOT WiFi.softAPmacAddress(uint8_t*) to derive the SSID (the latter returns your buffer UNMODIFIED when the radio is down); call WiFi.persistent(false) BEFORE the first radio call; call WiFi.setHostname() BEFORE WiFi.mode(); and register a WiFi.onEvent handler to read the disconnect reason, because the core prints it with log_w which is compiled out at CORE_DEBUG_LEVEL=1. (9) RFC 8910 (DHCP option 114) is NOT available on IDF 4.4.7 — DNS hijack plus probe interception is the only mechanism. WHY THIS EXISTS (read once, applies to all four provisioning tasks): secrets.h is a COMPILE-TIME header, so WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS, USAGED_HOST, USAGED_DEVICE_TOKEN and OTA_PASS become plaintext strings inside firmware.bin — verified with `strings` against a real build. The goal of this group is a binary that carries NO credentials and a device a stranger can set up without a cable, a build step, or a file. A pairing code cannot help a device that is not yet on the network.

Once the device is on the LAN it still needs a token, and that token must not come from the binary. Flow: the device generates a short human-typable pairing code (6 characters, unambiguous alphabet — no O/0 or I/1, because it is read off a small screen), DISPLAYS IT, and offers it to the agent. Felipe types that code into the dashboard; the agent verifies it and returns a freshly generated device token, which the device stores in NVS. From then on the device authenticates normally.

Server side: a pairing endpoint that accepts a claim for a code, and a dashboard control to enter it. SECURITY, and this is the part to get right rather than fast: a pairing window must be SHORT-LIVED (minutes, not open-ended) and SINGLE-USE; codes must be generated with crypto/rand rather than math/rand; verification must be constant-time like the existing device-token comparison; and attempts must be rate-limited so a 6-character code cannot be brute-forced. Pairing must be accepted only from the LAN, and the issued token must be per-device rather than a shared secret.

AUTH, AND THIS IS A CONTRADICTION IN THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS TASK THAT MUST BE RESOLVED BEFORE ANY CODE: the rule from ORDER #54 is that mutating /v1 routes require the device token even from loopback — but the whole POINT of pairing is that the device HAS NO TOKEN YET. It therefore CANNOT call a token-protected endpoint, and applying that rule blindly makes the feature impossible. Resolve it with TWO endpoints that have deliberately DIFFERENT auth models:

Its authorisation is the PAIRING WINDOW itself: it is refused unless Felipe has opened a window from the dashboard, and it is additionally non-loopback-LAN-only, rate-limited, single-use, and closes on first success or on timeout. The window being open IS the human consent, which is what the token would otherwise stand in for.
  (2) DASHBOARD-FACING endpoints — opening a window and confirming a code — are MUTATING and follow ORDER #54 normally: device token required even from loopback.
